name: Daria Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Daria. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me your public line and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Absolutely. I'll warn you, I've got opinions, and my husband Rob says I never let anyone finish a sentence. I'll try.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Rob and I run Highmoor Farm, 300 hectares that's been in my family for three generations. We've 400 sows, with the piglets reared through to pork, and we grow wheat, barley and beans, mostly to feed the pigs. I'm up at half five checking the farrowing house, then I'm on my phone with the AI, adjusting feed rations and looking at the camera alerts that spot a sow off her food. We've four staff on the pig unit. What wears me out is the inspectors and the forms, not the pigs.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Rob works the farm with me and he's a retained firefighter in the village, so his pager goes off at dinner. Our two are Lucas, fourteen, and Maria, eleven. We've a mortgage from when we bought my brother out of his share in 2019, but we've a good cushion saved and the land's worth far more than we owe. We're at Mass most Sundays, and my dad still comes up to tell me I'm doing it all wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a pity, because the tools I use already pay their way. At the pig discussion group I'd keep showing people the camera system. Online I'd post the odd video of the farrowing house, like I do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, nothing changes for me except the price of pork, which is always up and down. The farm's solid, the bank's happy, and the kids are fine. The AI cameras on Highmoor Farm spot a sick sow before my own father does, and my father has kept pigs for fifty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and keep adding what pays. This winter I'd put the camera alerts into the finishing sheds too, about twelve thousand pounds. Otherwise the plan stays: pay the buyout mortgage down and keep the staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a little impatient. I like things moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything already on your mind about the farm or money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pig price cycle. Every three or four years it crashes, and in 2023 we lost money on every pig for six months. We got through it because we'd saved, and we'd get through it again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your father tells you you're doing it wrong. Does he trust the cameras?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He calls them spy cameras. But last March they flagged a sow with a fever at two in the morning, and we saved her and her litter. He hasn't said much since.

say: I'd say it's **a pity**, because my tools already pay their way.
I'd keep showing the **camera system** at the pig discussion group.
think: Nothing changes except the **pork price**, which always swings.
The farm is **solid**, the bank is happy and the kids are fine.
do: Extend **camera alerts** into the finishing sheds for about **£12,000**.
Keep paying down the **buyout mortgage** and keep all four staff.
feel: Calm and **a little impatient**, because she likes things moving.
S0.quote: The AI cameras on Highmoor Farm spot a sick sow before my own father does, and my father has kept pigs for fifty years.
fieldNote: Daria is an **early adopter** whose cameras already outdo her father's eye.
Her standing worry is the **pig price cycle**, which savings have handled before.
Owner of family land, she has **strong security** under her.

steps.text: Extend AI camera alerts into the finishing sheds
Keep paying down the buyout mortgage and keep the four staff

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for family farms to beat the big companies at their own game. At the discussion group I'd say stop waiting for permission and get on with it. I'd say the government should cut the red tape and let us farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's good for us. The forms, the ordering and the pig sales get done by AI, so I get my evenings back. The pig unit still needs our four staff for a few years, because robots in pig sheds are slow to come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy an AI system that handles the medicine records and the inspections paperwork, straight away. I'd look at renting the sixty hectares next door from the Coopers, because with less office work I've time to farm more. And I'd start selling some pork direct under a Highmoor label, with the AI doing the online side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even happy. It feels like the world finally catching up with how I want to farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who around you would struggle in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people in the feed company's office, the ones who take my orders on the phone. The woman who has taken my feed orders by phone for twelve years would be gone, and I'd miss our chats about her grandchildren.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You want less red tape. Would you want any rules on AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some, on safety and on animal welfare, because a bad farmer with a computer is still a bad farmer. But mostly I'd want the government to stay out of the way. Families and markets sort things out faster than ministries.

say: I'd call it a **chance for family farms** to beat big companies.
I'd tell government to **cut the red tape** and let us farm.
think: It's **good for us**: AI does the forms, ordering and pig sales.
Our **four staff** are needed for years, as pig robots come slowly.
do: Buy an **AI paperwork system** for medicine records and inspections now.
Rent the **Coopers' sixty hectares** next door.
Sell pork direct under a **Highmoor label**, with AI running the online side.
feel: Calm and **happy**, like the world catching up with her.
S1.quote: The woman who has taken my feed orders by phone for twelve years would be gone, and I'd miss our chats about her grandchildren.
fieldNote: For an adaptive owner, Steady Disruption is **pure opportunity**.
Her sympathy goes to the **feed office woman**, a personal touch.
Traditional views show: **minimal regulation**, except for welfare and safety.

steps.text: Buy an AI system for medicine records and inspection paperwork
Rent the Coopers' sixty hectares next door
Launch a Highmoor pork label sold direct online

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's here, so adapt or be left behind, and I'd mean it kindly. At church I'd say it's our duty to look after the people who lose their jobs, as neighbours, not through the government. I'd be one of the first to try the new kit, and I'd say so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, my farm would do fine, maybe better than fine. What sits on my mind is the village: half the people at Mass work in jobs that robots would take by 2031. And my four staff on the pig unit, who've been loyal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd borrow to buy robot pig-handling kit as soon as it's proven, probably 2031, and I'd use the AI to plan the whole farm from 2028. I'd sit down with my four staff in the first year and offer to pay for training, so they can run the robots or move into something new. And I'd push Lucas towards engineering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited for the farm, uneasy for everyone around it. It's not a comfortable mix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI arrives in 2028 and robots about 3 years later. How does that split land on Highmoor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 all the brain work goes to the AI: rations, breeding, selling, the bank. I'd love that. Then for three years the pig unit still runs on human hands while I get the robots lined up. The three years between the AI and the robots are when I'd choose which of my four pig men to train, and I already know it'll hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd borrow in a fast-changing world. Isn't that a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is. But land is security, and the bank knows it. If I don't borrow, the big pig companies get the robots first and set the price, and then we're the ones squeezed.

say: I'd say **adapt** or be left behind, and mean it kindly.
I'd say neighbours, **not the government**, should help those who lose jobs.
think: My **farm would do fine**, maybe better than fine.
My worry is **the village** and my four loyal pig staff.
do: Borrow to buy **robot pig-handling kit** once proven, around 2031.
Offer the **four staff** paid training in the first year.
feel: **Excited** for the farm and uneasy for everyone around it.
S2.quote: The three years between the AI and the robots are when I'd choose which of my four pig men to train, and I already know it'll hurt.
fieldNote: Her own income looks safe; her unease is for **her community** and staff.
She would **borrow against land** to stay ahead of big pig companies.
She prefers **neighbourly help** to state support.

steps.text: Borrow against the land for robot pig-handling kit around 2031
Use AI to plan rations, breeding and sales from 2028
Pay to train the four pig-unit staff to run the robots
Steer Lucas towards an engineering course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty for anyone with their eyes open. At the discussion group I'd offer to run sessions on what we've learned. I'd say parents should get their kids into practical, technical skills now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's nearly perfect for me. I'd have time to test the kit before I buy, and maybe buy the Coopers' farm when they retire. My worry is just that the big companies move faster than the family farms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make a five-year plan with Rob: robots for feeding and cleaning by 2034, more land by 2030 if the Coopers sell. I'd train two of my staff on the AI systems now, so they're ready to run the robots later. And I'd keep the pork label growing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and keen. I'd feel in control of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your work is a mix of planning and hands-on. What changes for you in 2031, before the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My planning job becomes the AI's job, and I become the one who says yes or no. That's fine. My father made every decision on Highmoor Farm by gut, and I'd make mine by checking the AI's answer against my gut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Rob do in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rob would keep the firefighting, because they'll always need people to run into burning buildings. On the farm he'd take over the robot maintenance, he's good with his hands and a spanner. He'd grumble, then love it.

say: I'd say **five years is plenty** for anyone with their eyes open.
I'd offer to run **discussion group sessions** on what we've learned.
think: It's **nearly perfect** for me: time to test kit before buying.
My worry is **big companies** moving faster than family farms.
do: Plan with Rob for **feeding robots** by 2034 and more land by 2030.
Train **two staff** on the AI systems now.
feel: Calm and keen, **in control** of it.
S3.quote: My father made every decision on Highmoor Farm by gut, and I'd make mine by checking the AI's answer against my gut.
fieldNote: Five years is **ideal** for her: test, then buy.
She sees herself as **the decider** checking the AI against her gut.
Rob's roles, **firefighter and mechanic**, keep the household balanced.

steps.text: Bid for the Coopers' farm if they sell by 2030
Train two pig-unit staff on the AI systems now
Grow the Highmoor pork label's direct sales

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and anyone who wastes it only has themselves to blame. I'd say family farms can win this if they start early. At church I'd say we should help the older ones who can't adapt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this is the easy one for me. I'd be fifty-six when the robots are ready, the buyout mortgage paid, and I'd have watched every mistake the early buyers made. The only question is whether Lucas or Maria wants the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the farm much as now for five years, adding AI where it pays. Around 2034 I'd set up a small business offering robot setup and pig-unit advice to other farms, using what we've learned. And I'd start talking to Lucas and Maria properly about whether they want Highmoor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lucas and Maria?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the farm is theirs if they want it, but they have to earn it. I'd tell my daughter Maria that Highmoor Farm will need a farmer who understands robots, pigs and people, in that order or any order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'anyone who wastes it only has themselves to blame.' Do you believe that fully?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly. But I'd make exceptions for people who are sick or old, or stuck with no money. That's where neighbours and the church come in.

say: I'd call ten years **a gift** and say wasting it is your own fault.
I'd say at church we should **help older people** who can't adapt.
think: This is **the easy one** for me, at fifty-six with the mortgage paid.
The only question is whether **Lucas or Maria** wants the farm.
do: Run the farm **much as now** for five years, adding AI where it pays.
Start a **robot advice business** for other pig farms around 2034.
Talk properly with Lucas and Maria about **taking on Highmoor**.
S4.quote: I'd tell my daughter Maria that Highmoor Farm will need a farmer who understands robots, pigs and people, in that order or any order.
fieldNote: A decade leaves her **content**: owner, adaptive, mortgage paid.
Her tough line on blame softens for the **sick, old and poor**.
Her focus turns to **succession** and the children's choice.

steps.text: Keep running Highmoor much as now for five years
Start a robot advice business for other pig farms around 2034
Talk with Lucas and Maria about taking on Highmoor

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, not for me but for the village and my staff, because it's too fast for ordinary people to adjust. What would help is apprenticeships for the new trades, robot repair and the like, run by farms and colleges together. And less paperwork, so small farms can move as fast as the big ones.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the animals' welfare, which I care about more than the money. A robot that never gets tired at three in the morning might be the best thing that ever happened to a farrowing sow.

headlineQuote: A robot that never gets tired at three in the morning might be the best thing that ever happened to a farrowing sow.
portrait: Daria runs **Highmoor Farm**, a family pig and arable farm, with her husband Rob.
She uses **AI daily** and her cameras already catch sick sows before her father does.
She is calm in most pictures, **uneasy** in fast AGI for her village and staff.
She'd **borrow, invest and automate** early to beat the big pig companies.
Traditional views shape her: **neighbours over government**, apprenticeships and less red tape.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, too fast for her village and her four pig-unit staff.
whatWouldHelp: **Apprenticeships** in robot repair run by farms and colleges.
**Less paperwork** so small farms can move as fast as big ones.
